title: Debt Settlement vs Bankruptcy for Getting Out of Debt
metaDescription: Debt settlement vs bankruptcy compared on upfront fees, lawsuits, tax on forgiven debt, and how long each stays on your credit report, plus when each fits.
h1: Debt Settlement vs Bankruptcy for Debt You Cannot Repay
introText:
Debt settlement is a private deal where each creditor accepts less than you owe, while bankruptcy is a federal court case that can discharge eligible debts and stop collection. At The Modern Wallet, the mistake we see most often is comparing settlement's promised savings with court fees and ignoring its lawsuit and tax risks.

In settlement, each creditor decides the outcome, and the [Federal Trade Commission](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/how-get-out-debt) (FTC) says creditors have no obligation to negotiate. In bankruptcy, a court decides, and in Chapter 7 it must grant a discharge unless the law bars one.

Both paths damage your credit. Settlement usually involves months of missed payments, and a bankruptcy can stay on your credit report for up to 10 years.

verdict: Bankruptcy fits when your unsecured debt is more than you could repay in about five years, or when a creditor is already suing you. The automatic stay stops that collection once you file, and debt discharged in a Title 11 case is not taxable income. Debt settlement fits when you have cash for lump-sum offers, owe most of the debt to a few large unsecured creditors, and have assets you want to keep outside a bankruptcy case. The amount of cash you can raise for lump sums is the deciding condition. Without that money, settlement means more than a year of missed payments during which a creditor may sue, plus possible tax on whatever each creditor forgives. If you are not behind on payments yet, price a hardship plan with your card company or a nonprofit debt management plan before you choose either path.

sections.heading: Debt Settlement or Bankruptcy for Getting Out of Debt
sections.content:
Bankruptcy usually comes out ahead when your unsecured debt is more than you could repay in about five years, or when a creditor is already suing you. Filing a petition triggers the automatic stay in [Section 362 of Title 11](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/11/362) of the United States Code. The stay halts lawsuits, enforcement of judgments and other collection on debts from before the case, and debt canceled in a bankruptcy case is left out of your taxable income.

Debt settlement fits when you have cash on hand for lump-sum offers, owe most of your debt to a few large unsecured creditors, and hold assets you worry a bankruptcy case could put at risk. The [Consumer Financial Protection Bureau](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_quarterly-consumer-credit-trends_debt-settlement-credit-counseling_2020-07.pdf) (CFPB) found that settlements before charge-off typically happen when the consumer can pay one lump sum or finish paying within three months. Without that cash, settlement means letting accounts go unpaid while you save, and a creditor can sue you during that wait.

The five-year mark matches the longest a Chapter 13 repayment plan can run.

sections.heading: How Debt Settlement Works and Where It Goes Wrong
sections.content:
A debt settlement program usually advises you to stop paying your creditors and set aside money each month, then uses those savings to offer each creditor less than the balance. The FTC booklet [Choosing a Credit Counselor](https://consumer.ftc.gov/sites/default/files/articles/pdf/pdf-0040-choosing-a-credit-counselor.pdf) says these programs usually hold your savings in an escrow-like account and often tell clients to stop making monthly payments. The [CFPB's debt relief page](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-debt-relief-program-and-how-do-i-know-if-i-should-use-one-en-1457/) says settlement companies typically encourage you to stop paying your credit card bills.

Those missed payments cost money while you save. The CFPB says they usually bring late fees, penalty interest and other charges, and that working with a settlement company may lead to a collection lawsuit. The FTC adds that after 180 days without a payment, the creditor writes the debt off as a loss, your score takes a big hit, and you still owe the debt.

Reaching a settlement takes more than a year for a typical account. In the same CFPB report, the median account spent 13 months delinquent before settling through 2018, and 14 months in 2019. Most of those settlements came after charge-off, and most were agreed directly between the consumer and the debt holder.

The published completion figure is low. A 2010 [Government Accountability Office](https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-10-593t-highlights.pdf) (GAO) testimony said FTC and state investigations typically found that fewer than 10 percent of consumers completed these programs. That figure describes the market before the 2010 fee rule, and the CFPB reports that about 80 percent of settlement companies left the market after the rule took effect.

Treat any savings figure as a sales claim. Settlement companies say they negotiate 40 to 60 cents on the dollar, according to the [same GAO testimony](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-10-593t). The CFPB says settlement companies [cannot guarantee](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/archive/blog/coronavirus-and-dealing-debt-tips-help-ease-impact/) the amount or percentage you will save, and it warns that settlement may leave you deeper in debt than when you started.

sections.heading: How Bankruptcy Handles the Same Debts
sections.content:
Bankruptcy resolves your unsecured debts through one court order instead of a separate negotiation with each creditor. Under [Section 727 of Title 11](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/11/727), the court shall grant a Chapter 7 discharge unless one of the listed bars applies. That discharge covers debts that arose before the order for relief, subject to the exceptions in [Section 523](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/11/523).

Chapter 13 works through a repayment plan. [U.S. Courts](https://www.uscourts.gov/court-programs/bankruptcy/bankruptcy-basics/chapter-13-bankruptcy-basics) says plans usually run three to five years and can never exceed five, and [Section 1328](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/11/1328) grants the discharge after you finish the plan payments. U.S. Courts also calls the Chapter 13 discharge somewhat broader than Chapter 7's, and Chapter 13 lets you catch up on missed mortgage payments over time to save a home from foreclosure.

Each chapter has entry limits. Chapter 13 requires unsecured debts below $526,700 and secured debts below $1,580,125, and Chapter 7 bars a discharge if you received one in a case started within the previous eight years. Our [Chapter 7 vs Chapter 13 comparison](/compare/chapter-7-vs-chapter-13-bankruptcy/) covers how the two chapters differ for income and property.

Some debts survive either chapter. Section 523 keeps domestic support obligations, certain taxes, debts from fraud or willful and malicious injury, and certain government fines. It also keeps student loans unless repaying them would impose an undue hardship.

Recent spending can also stay with you. Luxury purchases over $900 from one creditor within 90 days before the case, and cash advances over $1,250 within 70 days, are presumed nondischargeable. Before you file under either chapter, the FTC says you must complete credit counseling with a government-approved organization within the previous six months, and the [U.S. Trustee Program list](https://www.justice.gov/ust/list-credit-counseling-agencies-approved-pursuant-11-usc-111) names the approved agencies.

sections.heading: What Each Path Costs Before You Get Relief
sections.content:
A for-profit debt settlement company that sells by phone cannot charge you until it has settled at least one of your debts and you have made at least one payment under that deal. The rule comes from the FTC's Telemarketing Sales Rule (TSR), in Title 16 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) at [section 310.4](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/16/310.4). It protects anyone who enrolled in a debt relief service after October 27, 2010.

The TSR also controls how the company handles your fees and your savings:

- Each fee must match that debt's share of your total enrolled debt, or be a percentage of the amount saved that stays the same for every debt.
- If the company requires a dedicated account, your savings must sit at an insured financial institution, in an account you own, run by an administrator with no ties to the settlement company.
- You can withdraw at any time without penalty and get your money back, minus fees already earned, within seven business days.
- Before you sign, [16 CFR 310.3](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/16/310.3) requires the company to tell you how long results will take and how much you must save before it makes an offer. It must also warn you that missed payments can hurt your credit and bring lawsuits.

The TSR has a gap for nonprofits. The [FTC's 2010 announcement](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2010/10/debt-relief-companies-prohibited-collecting-advance-fees-under-ftc-rule-takes-effect-october-27-2010) says it does not cover nonprofit firms, though it does cover companies that falsely claim nonprofit status. The FTC also warns that nonprofit status does not guarantee a service is free or affordable, so get any fee quote in writing before you enroll. The FTC's [March 2026 scam alert](https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/03/looking-debt-relief-heres-how-avoid-scam) says only scammers ask for payment before settling any debt, and anyone who guarantees to settle all your debts is a scammer.

Neither the FTC nor the CFPB publishes a typical settlement fee. The CFPB says only that settlement companies often charge expensive fees. Bankruptcy carries court fees and requires a credit counseling course before filing, and our guide to [what it costs to file bankruptcy](/guides/how-much-does-it-cost-to-file-bankruptcy/) has the current fee figures.

sections.heading: How Taxes Differ in Debt Settlement vs Bankruptcy
sections.content:
Debt forgiven in a settlement is generally taxable income, while debt discharged in a bankruptcy case is excluded. The [Internal Revenue Service](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc431) (IRS) lists debt canceled in a Title 11 bankruptcy case among its exclusions. [IRS Publication 4681](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p4681) gives the settlement case: you owe $1,000, pay $400 to settle the whole debt, and have $600 of canceled debt to report as income.

The income counts even if no tax form arrives. A creditor generally files Form 1099-C when it cancels $600 or more of a debt, according to the [IRS instructions for Form 1099-C](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1099ac). Publication 4681 says you report canceled debt as income without that form unless an exception or exclusion applies.

One exclusion outside bankruptcy is insolvency. Under [Section 108 of the tax code](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/108), you can exclude canceled debt only up to the amount by which your total liabilities exceeded the fair market value of all your assets just before the cancellation. You claim it by attaching Form 982 to your federal return and checking line 1b.

Run the arithmetic before you accept a settlement. Say your liabilities total $40,000 and your assets are worth $30,000 just before a creditor forgives $15,000. You are insolvent by $10,000, so $10,000 of the forgiven amount is excluded and the other $5,000 is taxable income.

sections.heading: How Long Each Path Stays on Your Credit Report
sections.content:
A settled delinquent account can stay on your credit report for about seven and a half years from the first missed payment, while a bankruptcy case can stay for up to 10 years. Under the [Fair Credit Reporting Act](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1681c) (FCRA), charged-off and collection accounts drop off after seven years, and that clock starts 180 days after the delinquency began. Seven years plus 180 days comes to about seven and a half years. The bankruptcy clock runs from the order for relief.

The FCRA has no separate rule for settlements. A settled account that went delinquent falls under the same seven-year limit, and CFPB data shows credit records can identify accounts reported as settled for less than the full balance. The [CFPB's credit report page](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-long-does-information-stay-on-my-credit-report-en-323/) states the general rule as seven years for most negative items and up to ten for bankruptcies.

The time limits do not cover every credit check. They do not apply to reports pulled for credit of $150,000 or more, or for a job paying $75,000 or more.

Both paths can hurt your credit. The CFPB says settlement can lower your credit scores, and the [National Foundation for Credit Counseling](https://www.nfcc.org/blog/debt-relief-programs-the-pros-and-cons-of-each-type/) (NFCC) says on its own site that scores can drop 100 points or more. Our guide to [what a good credit score is](/guides/what-is-a-good-credit-score/) explains the ranges, and [how to build credit fast](/guides/how-to-build-credit-fast/) covers rebuilding after either path.

sections.heading: Who Debt Settlement Fits and Who Bankruptcy Fits
sections.content:
Debt settlement fits a household that can fund lump-sum offers, owes most of its unsecured debt to a few large creditors, and wants to keep its assets out of a bankruptcy case. That household also needs room for a tax bill on the forgiven amount, or enough insolvency to exclude it. Settlement is a poor fit if a creditor has already sued you, because the automatic stay that halts lawsuits comes from a bankruptcy filing.

Bankruptcy fits a household whose debt is larger than five years of payments could cover, or one facing a lawsuit or a judgment it cannot pay. It also fits someone who could not absorb a tax bill on forgiven debt.

Bankruptcy does little for debts that Section 523 keeps, such as support or student loans without an undue-hardship finding. Our guide on [how to pay off debt](/guides/how-to-pay-off-debt/) covers repaying those debts. A new Chapter 7 discharge is also unavailable within eight years of a case that ended in one.

If you are not behind yet, price the lighter options before either path. The FTC says you can negotiate with a creditor yourself for free, and the [CFPB says many card companies](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-should-i-do-if-i-cant-pay-my-credit-card-bills-en-1697/) are willing to work with you to change your payment during a financial emergency. [Get written confirmation](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/archive/blog/need-help-your-credit-card-debt-start-your-credit-card-company/) of any new payment plan you agree to.

A debt management plan (DMP) through a nonprofit credit counselor rolls your unsecured debts into one monthly payment that the counselor sends to your creditors. The FTC says a DMP could take 48 months or more to finish. Our [bankruptcy alternatives guide](/guides/bankruptcy-alternatives/) compares a DMP with direct negotiation and consolidation.

Income from Social Security or veterans benefits has its own protections from collectors. The CFPB says a debt collector must [sue and win a judgment](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/can-a-debt-collector-take-my-social-security-or-va-benefits-en-1157/) before taking those benefits, and two months of directly deposited benefits stay protected in your bank account. For wages, the [Department of Labor](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/30-cppa) says no garnishment is allowed when weekly disposable earnings are $217.50 or less, and our guide on [dealing with debt collectors](/guides/how-to-deal-with-debt-collectors/) covers your other rights.

sections.heading: What Would Change Our Answer on Debt Settlement vs Bankruptcy
sections.content:
New federal data on how settlement programs perform would change our answer more than anything else. The fewer-than-10-percent completion figure comes from the market before the 2010 advance-fee rule, and most settlement companies left that market afterward. A current federal study showing that most people who enroll finish with savings after fees and taxes would widen the group settlement fits.

Two tax changes would also move us. Removing the Title 11 exclusion from Section 108 would take away bankruptcy's tax advantage. A broad exclusion for all settled consumer debt would remove settlement's tax cost, which we would then weigh against its lawsuit risk.

Neither change is in the law in 2026. List each unsecured debt with its balance and whether a creditor has sued. Then run your monthly numbers through the [Budget Calculator](/budget/) to see what you could set aside for lump sums.

Courts, trustees and local rules vary, so a bankruptcy attorney, a legal-aid office or a nonprofit credit counselor can apply these rules to your own debts.

faqs.question: Is debt settlement better than bankruptcy?
faqs.answer: Debt settlement is better than bankruptcy only in a narrow case: you have cash for lump-sum offers, your creditors are willing to deal, and you can handle tax on the forgiven amount. The FTC says creditors have no obligation to negotiate, and GAO testimony in 2010 reported that fewer than 10 percent of consumers finished settlement programs. A bankruptcy, on the other hand, can stay on your credit report for up to 10 years.

faqs.question: Does debt settlement hurt your credit as much as bankruptcy?
faqs.answer: A settled account usually stays on your credit report for less time than a bankruptcy, though both lower your score. The FCRA limits charged-off and collection accounts to seven years, starting 180 days after the first missed payment, which comes to about seven and a half years. A bankruptcy case can be reported for up to 10 years. The NFCC says settlement can drop scores by 100 points or more, and the FTC says a debt written off after 180 days of nonpayment hits your score hard.

faqs.question: Can a creditor sue me during debt settlement?
faqs.answer: Yes, a creditor can sue you during debt settlement, and the CFPB says working with a settlement company may lead to a collection lawsuit. Old debts are the exception: under [Regulation F](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1006/26/), a collector cannot sue or threaten to sue on a debt past its statute of limitations. The CFPB says a partial payment may restart that clock, so read its [page on old debts](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/can-debt-collectors-collect-a-debt-thats-several-years-old-en-1423/) before paying on an account that is several years old. Calls can continue during a program, though the CFPB says collectors are [generally barred](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/when-and-how-often-can-a-debt-collector-call-me-on-the-phone-en-2110/) from calling before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m.

faqs.question: Do I have to pay taxes on settled debt?
faqs.answer: Yes, settled debt is generally taxable income unless an exclusion applies. The IRS treats the forgiven part as income, so paying $400 to settle a $1,000 debt leaves $600 to report. You report it even if the creditor never sends Form 1099-C. If your liabilities exceeded the value of your assets just before the cancellation, you can exclude the forgiven amount up to that gap by filing Form 982. Debt discharged in a Title 11 bankruptcy case is excluded entirely.

faqs.question: What's the difference between debt consolidation and debt settlement?
faqs.answer: Debt consolidation replaces several debts with one new loan you repay in full, while debt settlement tries to get part of each debt forgiven. The [CFPB's comparison page](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-the-difference-between-credit-counseling-and-debt-settlement-debt-consolidation-or-credit-repair-en-1449/) warns that a low consolidation rate may be a teaser rate that lasts only a limited time. A home equity loan used to consolidate can cost you the house in foreclosure if you stop paying it. With settlement, the CFPB says the forgiven amount could leave you owing taxes. Our [Debt Consolidation Calculator](/debt-consolidation-calculator/) shows what one new loan would cost you each month.
